fields.sections.0.h: Sudden collapse of an online infrastructure built over 25 years
fields.sections.1.h: Legitimacy of the .name domain: differences from typical 3rd-level domains
fields.sections.2.h: Verisign trust issue: historical background of corporate acquisition
fields.sections.3.h: Direct damage from domain deletion: simultaneous loss of website, email, and IoT devices
fields.sections.4.h: Greater risk: domain hijacking and identity theft potential
fields.sections.5.h: Beyond individual impact: collective harm to 22,000 users
fields.sections.0.ko: The author registered the neil.fraser.name domain approximately 25 years ago, making it the hub of online activities including website, email, and API servers. Having operated this domain since before YouTube and Facebook existed, it held significant personal meaning—the author even registered beverly.fraser.name on the day his daughter was born. However, on April 15, 2026, domain manager Verisign proposed the complete deletion of all 3rd-level (3rd-level) .name domains, and surprisingly, ICANN approved it on July 28.
fields.sections.1.ko: 3rd-level domains generally have a reputation for low trustworthiness. For example, domains like *.uk.co are where individual entrepreneurs purchase a country domain (Colombia's .co) and resell it, and when that entrepreneur disappears, the domain disappears too. However, .name has a completely different structure. It was designed exclusively for 3rd-level use from the start, xxx.yyy.name can be registered through any registrar, and complete whois records exist. This is identical to standard domain systems like *.ny.us or *.co.uk.
fields.sections.2.ko: One of the original reasons the author chose .name was because it was operated by Global Name Registry. It was important that an entity other than Verisign manage it—the author did not trust that company due to past dealings. Unfortunately, years later Verisign acquired Global Name Registry, and the numerous false claims included in this deletion proposal vindicated the author's original concerns.
fields.sections.3.ko: Upon domain deletion in February 2026, the author's website disappears immediately. This occurs despite the domain being registered until 2040 and payment already made. The email address is also lost, and all IoT devices using this domain's services become inoperable. Ultimately, the author's trace on the internet vanishes.
fields.sections.4.ko: After deletion, when 2nd-level domains become available for re-registration, someone other than the author could purchase fraser.name and recreate and control neil.fraser.name. This would allow hijacking of hundreds of online accounts opened with this email address, performing code commits with the author's authentication, or taking control of IoT devices. Because there is no way to identify all accounts opened with this email over 25 years, the extent of damage cannot be known at all.
fields.sections.5.ko: The author is merely one of 22,000 users who will be harmed by this domain deletion. It is a scale of collective damage that individual users cannot bear, and the author has indicated willingness to consider legal measures in response to this issue.
fields.caveat: The article contains only the author's personal account and the fact of ICANN approval, and verification is needed regarding Verisign's stated reasons for deletion, official rebuttal to those reasons, current status of legal disputes, and other matters.
